title: Free energies and optimal reaction coordinates via entropy production
authors: Jérémy Diharce, Line Mouaffac, Axel Dian, Fabio Pietrucci
abstract: We show through theory and numerical experiments that a straightforward calculation of entropy production on short molecular dynamics trajectories allows estimating free-energy barriers and identifying optimal reaction coordinates of activated processes. To this aim, we perform an analysis based on stochastic energetics on a set of trajectories relaxing towards equilibrium from a same initial configuration, projected on different putative coordinates. After demonstrating the approach on simple benchmarks, we show that it is possible to estimate the free-energy barrier of a complex high-dimensional system (carbon nanoparticles in water) and to rank the quality of order parameters, in agreement with the committor probability. The results shed light on the entanglement between the second law, free-energy landscapes, reaction coordinates and kinetic rates.
summary: This paper introduces a method to estimate free-energy barriers and find optimal reaction coordinates by analyzing the total entropy production ($\Delta S_{tot}$) during molecular dynamics simulations. By leveraging stochastic energetics, the authors show that $\Delta S_{tot}$ calculated from short trajectories provides an accurate measure of the free energy difference, even in complex, high-dimensional systems like nanoparticles in water.
main_problem: The work aims to estimate free-energy barriers and identify optimal reaction coordinates for activated processes by calculating total entropy production ($\Delta S_{tot}$) from short molecular dynamics trajectories.
main_result: Calculating $\Delta S_{tot}$ via stochastic energetics provides a robust method that successfully estimates free-energy barriers, with the committor function yielding results consistent with theoretical expectations.
method: The core methodology involves applying stochastic energetics to Langevin trajectories to calculate $\Delta S_{tot}$, which is related to the free energy difference ($\Delta F$) by $\Delta F = -T\Delta S_{tot}$.
model_or_system: Benchmarks include 1D double-well potentials and 2D systems, culminating in a complex test case: carbon nanoparticles (C60) interacting with water molecules.
key_observables: Total entropy production ($\Delta S_{tot}$), free energy profile ($ eta F(q)$), committor probability ($\phi$), and the ratio $\log(P_{end}/P_{begin})$.
important_parameters: Temperature (T=300 K), time step ($\Delta t$), and the relationship between entropy production and free energy barriers.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system operates in the overdamped regime, and when projecting to a single coordinate, it assumes fast equilibration of orthogonal degrees of freedom.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the connection between relaxation dynamics, $\Delta S_{tot}$, and free-energy differences; they compare $\Delta S_{tot}$ estimates from various coordinates against the committor probability, confirming its optimality.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the theoretical link ($\Delta F = -T\Delta S_{tot}$) using stochastic energetics on simple benchmarks (1D double-well), then extending this to multi-dimensional systems and finally applying it to a complex biomolecular system like C60 in water.
why_interesting: The direct connection established between the second law of thermodynamics ($\Delta S_{tot}$) and free energy landscapes provides an alternative, potentially more robust, pathway for calculating reaction barriers than traditional methods relying solely on potential energy surfaces or sampling equilibrium distributions.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Illustrative example of the connection between relaxation processes, entropy production, and free-energy dif- ferences. Several trajectories are shown, evolving on a free- energy landscape F(x, y) from an initial state (high free en- ergy) to a final state (low free energy). According to ther- modynamics, any spontaneous relaxation process entails an increase in total entropy T∆Stot = −∆F. However, when observed from the viewpoint of a generic single variable q, the free-energy drop and the entropy production appear re- duced from the true value, due to properties of the marginal probability density ρ(q) = e−βF (q)/Z, unless an optimal pro- jection coordinate (here x) is employed.

Figure 5. Measured entropy production rate of equilibrium trajectories, varying the number of points per bin Nb and the timestep ∆t. Data points represent the time average over 1500 steps of 10000 independent trajectories sampling the equilibrium ensemble of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process where F(q) = −q and D = 1. Because the true EPR at equilibrium is identically zero, the non-zero measured values stem entirely from finite-data bias, collapsing onto the predicted scaling law ˙Stot = 1/(Nb∆t).
